To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the back-door criterion can be generalized to more general graphs and that there are graphical criteria for the generalized criterion.

(1) Pearl’s back-door adjustment criterion can be generalized to more general types (Markov equivalence classes) of causal graphs and (2) there exist graphical criteria that are necessary and sufficient for the existence of an adjustment set that satisfies the generalized back-door criterion.

the generalized back-door criterion is necessary and sufficient for the existence of an unconfounded estimate of the causal effect of an exposure variable on an outcome variable, when considering a set of variables as controls.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification problem in structural causal models, i.e. with determining under what circumstances the effect of interventions on the probability distribution of observed variables can be identified from observational data.
the problem of finding sufficient statistics for causal parameters in graphical models.
the following question: When is it true that a causal effect can be identified from observational data, even though the causal graph is unfaithful?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our results are not only a theoretical contribution, but they also provide a practical method for the identification of causal effects.

the generalized back-door criterion can be applied in the same way as Pearl’s back-door condition, except that the set of variables that satisfy the generalized back-door condition is not necessarily unique.
our generalized back-door criteria are the most general ones that are known to us, and that they are easy to check and to implement in practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

our generalized back-door condition provides an answer to the following question: Given a graph G and two variables, say X and Y, which of the following statements are true: 1) There exists a set of back-door variables that satisfies the back-door criterion, 2) There exists a subset of variables that satisfies the criterion, and 3) There exists a minimal subset of variables that fulfills the condition.
we have developed an algorithm that finds the optimal backdoor set for any given graph, and we have developed a graphical criterion that tells us when the backdoor set is unique.
we generalize the graphical back-door criterion from Pearl (1995), which is only applicable to DAGs and only for one intervention, to a larger class of causal graphs and multiple interventions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when considering a set of variables as a potential set of confounders, the back-door criterion is more general and more robust than previously thought.
the back-door criterion can be generalized to more general graphs and that the generalized criterion is easier to check than the original one.

in many cases, the graphical criterion for the existence of the set of variables satisfying the backdoor criterion is simpler than the corresponding graphical criterion for the d-separation criterion.
